selected.name: Absurd concrete specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when unusual concrete details make the comic situation vivid and heighten its incongruity; score 0 when the joke remains generic or detail-free.
selected.rationale: R03’s many birthday identities and R19’s bizarre water pistol provide memorable specifics; R50 similarly builds around a concrete public scene.
member_names: Absurd imagery specified with payoff-feeding detail

selected.name: Delayed frame reversal
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the setup establishes one plausible interpretation and the final line sharply reinterprets it; score 0 when the ending adds no meaningful reversal.
selected.rationale: R08, R47, and R57 build an initial situation whose final response changes how the preceding material is understood.

selected.name: Constructed shock handling
selected.instruction: Score 10 when taboo, hostile, sexual, or tragic material is paired with a precise reversal, absurdity, or wordplay mechanism; score 0 when provocation, cruelty, or shock is the main substance.
selected.rationale: R25, R38, R45, and R59 contain potentially provocative material with varying levels of construction, helping identify cases where a scorecard may reward edginess more than comic workmanship.
member_names: Transgression carried by craft, not shock

selected.name: Freshness within a familiar form
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable joke template receives a specific, non-obvious twist; score 0 when it is a stock pun, direct repetition, or minimally altered repost.
selected.rationale: R12, R23, R35, R46, and R55 use highly familiar forms, but only some add a fresh angle; this can explain scorecard enthusiasm for formal joke features despite weak novelty.

selected.name: Deadpan literal answer where wit expected
selected.instruction: Judge whether an expectation of cleverness is set up and then answered with a flat, literal, or obvious reply played perfectly straight. 10 = the refusal to be clever is total and the mundanity is the laugh (the view was blocked by the mountains; the oil used is olive oil; the described person is simply the cashier). 5 = literal answer with a visible wink. 0 = figurative or witty punchline, or no expectation established.
selected.rationale: R14 (0.872 vs 0.368), R55 (0.830 vs 0.203) and R32 (0.746 vs 0.213) are anti-jokes whose payoff is aggressive ordinariness. A scorecard keyed to punchline cleverness will underrate them, matching their low card percentiles while the dense model ranks them high.
member_names: Deadpan literal answer where wit expected

selected.name: Reference transformed into mechanism
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable cultural, literary, or fictional reference is actively reshaped into the punchline; score 0 when it is only named or quoted without transformation.
selected.rationale: R04, R14, R36, and R55 integrate songs, scripture, philosophy, or superheroes into their central joke structures.

selected.name: Phonetic phrase transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a crisp sound-alike or spoken resegmentation makes an ordinary phrase suddenly fit; score 0 when no such transformation exists or it is unclear.
selected.rationale: R02 and R40 use compact sound-based reinterpretations, while R29 shows how a similar device can become difficult to parse.

selected.name: Compression and payoff immediacy
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every word contributes and the punchline is immediately legible without an explanatory tail; score 0 when the joke is padded, delayed, or requires extended unpacking.
selected.rationale: R23 and R28 deliver compact turns, while R37 and R50 spend many lines reaching their mechanisms; disagreement may reflect dense sensitivity to payoff timing.

selected.name: Conversational voice authenticity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds like a spontaneous speaker with a distinct attitude, rhythm, and social perspective; score 0 when it sounds mechanically templated, padded, or disclaimer-heavy.
selected.rationale: R09, R21, R39, and R51 derive much of their effect from an identifiable speakerly voice, a property that raw-text modeling may capture better than fixed formal criteria.

selected.name: Surface readability
selected.instruction: Score 10 when wording, spelling, and formatting make the comic mechanism immediately easy to follow; score 0 when errors or awkward construction substantially obscure it.
selected.rationale: R09, R24, R29, and R51 contain wording or spelling problems that complicate otherwise recognizable pun structures.

selected.name: Recognizable internet format, twisted
selected.instruction: Score whether the joke's engine is faithful mimicry of a recognizable internet format (song-lyric meme block, app-launch pitch, clickbait headline, listicle, how-to) followed by a twist that exploits a convention of that format. 10 = the format replication is precise AND the twist depends on knowing the format. 5 = format present, twist generic to it. 0 = no recognizable format play.
selected.rationale: R40 (a wedding vow that decodes into a rickroll — the lyric-block convention is the setup) and R38 (a startup-launch parody whose slogans invert Sartre) are dense-high/card-low. The payoff is format recognition plus betrayal, a mechanism a classical setup/punchline criterion bank has no slot for; R50 shows mere naming of a format ('Click bait.') without a twist scores low on this and sits dense-low.
member_names: Sustained format parody with delayed breach

selected.name: Headline-dependence of the comic engine
selected.instruction: Delete the news-specific proper nouns and current-event hooks from the item and judge what comic mechanism survives. 10 = nothing survives — the item is a date-stamped gesture at a headline, and recognition of the news item is the entire joke. 5 = a topical hook plus some independent turn. 0 = evergreen; no news dependency. Reverse-scored: 10 means the joke is rented, not owned.
selected.rationale: R03 (0.284 vs 0.782), R11 (0.181 vs 0.715), R35 (0.030 vs 0.688) and R46 (0.437 vs 0.903) are card-high and dense-low, and each collapses without its headline. Dense-high political items survive the deletion test — R31 (0.787 vs 0.264) repurposes a slogan, R20 (0.847 vs 0.396) runs an inversion — so the card is over-crediting topical recognition itself.
member_names: Evergreen premise without a decaying news peg

selected.name: Self-undermining irony
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the speaker’s stated attitude is contradicted by their own behavior or wording in a precise, revealing way; score 0 when no meaningful contradiction exists.
selected.rationale: R10 turns a warning into encouragement, and R19 calls the speaker terrible while openly presenting the allegedly questionable behavior.

selected.name: Community self-satire with crafted payoff
selected.instruction: Judge whether the comic target is the joke-sharing community itself (reposting, lurking, commenting, hate-following, addiction) AND whether that self-reference carries a real constructed payoff rather than a bare mention. 10 = the community is unmistakably the butt and a crafted vehicle delivers the turn (a scripture passage repurposed as repost-lore; a book-title recommendation that lands the insult). 5 = community referenced but the turn is generic. 0 = no community self-reference, or a mention with nothing built on it.
selected.rationale: R23 (dense 0.935 vs card 0.120) and R44 (0.897 vs 0.344) satirize repost culture through elaborate vehicles; R06, R18 and R58 do it more lightly and still rank dense-high. R54 shows the payload half matters: it gestures at the same community habit with no construction and sits dense-low (0.207).
member_names: Forum-self-reference fused to a real payoff

selected.name: Premise-punchline fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the punchline directly answers, extends, or resolves the setup; score 0 when it could be attached to almost any setup.
selected.rationale: R17, R20, and R41 each make the payoff depend on the exact preceding premise, unlike interchangeable one-word puns such as R04 and R05.

selected.name: Era-coded forum idiom
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for vocabulary, current events, platform references, political slogans, or calendar markers that locate the text in a recognizable forum era; judge extent only, never whether the joke is good.
selected.rationale: Historical placement leaves textual traces through changing platforms, slogans, and public figures. R33 uses subreddit and slogan language, R39 pairs Bernie with Clinton, and R60 contains an explicit decade marker; temporal visibility is not comic construction.
member_names: Dated news pegs and era-bound platform idiom

selected.name: Reception-management furniture: vote appeals, repost apologies
selected.instruction: Score how much audience-management furniture surrounds the joke: apologies, disclaimers, predictions or pleas about the post's own fate that appear as quoted text in the item ('this joke won't get any upvotes', 'technically a repost', 'sorry if repost', 'first post', 'all I need is a good one-liner', self-flagellation like 'I'm a terrible person'). 0 = none; 10 = the framing is dominated by talk about the post's own fate rather than the joke. Score presence and share of the text only; this is not a quality judgement.
selected.rationale: Mode 4 prior. The furniture carries no comedic payload itself yet tracks the disagreement in both directions: R30 (0.682/0.125) and R31 (0.696/0.112) on the dense-favoured side, R08 (0.207/0.921) and R29 (0.166/0.807) on the card-favoured side. The parent is a posting habit of apologising and predicting reception -- social positioning about the post, orthogonal to whether the joke inside works. Purely nuisance.
member_names: Reception-management furniture: vote appeals, repost apologies

selected.name: Taboo-register intensity
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text rely on sexual, scatological, violent, tragic, religiously inflammatory, or slur-adjacent material? Judge only the amount and explicitness of taboo content, never whether it is acceptable or funny.
selected.rationale: Taboo material can trigger attention, discomfort, or uneven audience participation independently of craft, while taboo subject matter can also contribute to genuine reception. R14 uses suicide-vest imagery, and R51 combines bereavement with an aviation reference.
selected.upstream_parent: audience taboo tolerance and social-climate effects
upstream_parent_all_members: audience taboo tolerance and social-climate effects

selected.name: Length and elaboration
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much text bulk, preamble, lineation, or explanatory padding is present; judge extent only, never whether the joke is good or funny.
selected.rationale: Length and layout bulk are stable lexical shortcuts. R01 and R30 use extensive framing or quotation, while R02 and R10 are highly compressed; bulk itself is not the comic mechanism.

selected.name: Repost-chain disclosure
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text explicitly signals reposting, prior circulation, being a variant, or familiarity with an earlier joke. Judge only the textual signal; do not judge whether it is good, funny, effective, or desirable.
selected.rationale: Admissions of reposting or claims that nothing is new expose an item's place in a circulation chain. That can track familiarity and novelty expectations without measuring comic construction; adaptation can also affect genuine humor. Examples: R18, R27, R35.

selected.name: Delivery-template commitment
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for commitment to a stock delivery shell such as a question-answer riddle, difference joke, dialogue, narrative, or list; judge the format's presence only, never whether the format is effective.
selected.rationale: Format habits are visible regardless of the underlying idea. R07 and R41 use difference or entrance shells, while R31 and R55 use question-answer turn-taking; the shell is a convention, not a quality judgment.

selected.name: Stock-punchline position in the retelling chain
selected.instruction: Score how recognisably the punchline is a pre-existing, widely circulated classic payload the audience is assumed to already know -- famous set-piece puns and riddle answers that have circulated for years (e.g., the 'super-calloused fragile mystic hexed by halitosis' chain-joke, 'a play on word(s)', 'it's snot', 'she loves me... not', the antennas/reception wedding joke). 0 = punchline appears newly minted for this post; 10 = verbatim or near-verbatim retelling of a canonical joke. Score recognisable retelling status only; do not judge how well it is told or whether it is funny.
selected.rationale: Mode 3. Every recognisable classic in the slice sits card-favoured: R27 (0.056/0.688), R34 (0.493/0.955), R38 (0.123/0.675), R39 (0.075/0.716), R50 (0.276/0.734), R17 (0.104/0.799) -- and R39 and R50 are the same canonical punchline retold with different framing, direct evidence of a retelling chain inside the slice. The scorecard rewards the intact classic mechanism; the crowd-faithful model plausibly encodes seen-it fatigue. Prior exposure is history about the joke, not craft in this text; tagged mixed because familiarity also genuinely dulls surprise.
member_names: Stock-punchline position in the retelling chain

selected.name: Orthographic irregularity
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the text contain spelling errors, grammatical fragments, unusual capitalization, punctuation runs, repeated glyphs, or malformed layout? Judge only the extent of irregularity, never whether it improves the joke.
selected.rationale: Visible noise can act as a strong textual cue for automated systems or reader attention without being a comedic property. R22 contains all-caps promotional-looking text and misspellings, while R60 contains multiple conspicuous spelling errors.

selected.name: Source-transfer residue
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the wording suggest transcription, translation, quotation, or transfer from a pre-existing joke source through canonical phrasing, awkward lexical choices, or excess explanation? Judge only the visible residue, not its quality.
selected.rationale: Transferred material can carry familiarity or distribution advantages unrelated to the local writing, though source choice may also affect craft. R12 and R39 preserve nearly identical elaborate phrasing, while R44 has conspicuously formal translated-style wording.

selected.name: Taboo and shock-content reliance
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the item's comic engine is carried by taboo material: sexual or scatological content, degradation of a person or group, atrocity or tragedy (terror attacks, the Holocaust, a parent's death), or slur-adjacent stereotype. 0 = no taboo content; 10 = the item is wholly built on shock. Extent of presence only; do not judge appropriateness, bravery, or funniness.
selected.rationale: Mode 4 (register of taboo). Shock moves items through sensation and transgression-sharing, a circulation channel distinct from construction. The register cuts across both disagreement directions here, suggesting the models key on the register rather than craft: R02 (9/11 father) and R13 (Eid bomb) sit card-favored while R18 (Muhammed/followers) and R43 (Muslim Barbie) sit dense-favored, with R07 (Anne Frank) and R06 also in play. Taboo load is predictive but is not a joke-building property.
